newsitem.title: UK: Asian demand steadies W.African crudes, Med quiet.
newsitem.headline: Asian demand steadies W.African crudes, Med quiet.

text.p: Asian interest kept permiums for West African crude steady on Monday while the Russian market in the Mediterranean showed signs of softening, traders said.

"They(differentials) are holding up, if not getting stronger," one seller of African barrels said, adding Bonny Light was in the Dated Brent +40/+45 cents region, Qua Iboe perhaps a few pennies lower and Forcados at Dated Brent +5/+10 cents.

Up to six cargoes of Bonny Light and Medium, Forcados and possibly Brass River -- mostly loading second or third decade of May -- were heard to have been snatched up last week by South Korean, Taiwanese, and Indonesian buyers.
"They (Asians) seem to be keeping up their interest and there's a lot of talk," he said, adding "quiet a few" VLCCs of Nigerian grades, mostly end April cargoes, were heading to the U.S. Gulf.
"Summer is approaching and there is U.S. interest in gasoline-rich grades. Certainly Nigerian grades are on top of the list," he added.
About five Nigerian crude cargoes were also picked up by some European buyers early last week, a refiner said.
In the Mediterranean, no deals were reported on Monday but a European refiner bought a Urals cargo on Friday. Reports of the price ranged between Dated Brent -$1.05 and -$1.08.
Earlier trades said that there might be one or two cargoes of the Russian crude yet to shown in the first decade of May.
A trader said Urals was being talked at about Dated Brent -$1.05/$1.10 cif but is starting to come off a little bit as it was a bit hyped up at the end of last week.
"It started to get closer to real market values... Some traders were trying to push it up to nearly $1 (below Dated Brent) but it never traded there," he added.

"I think Urals should come off a little bit...It will be pressure from (Iraqi) Kirkuk...and it (Urals) was a bit hyped up because there were much delays at the end of April so the market came up. Let's hope that in May it will be a little bit easier," the trader said.

Another trader backed the view that the short-term outlook for the sour crude would be a bit bearish, saying pressure would come from the approach of summer, when demand dips for Urals, which produces less gasoline than sweeter crudes.
- Haitham Haddadin, London newroom +44 171 542 8145 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
